title: Microsoft Opens Largest India Data Centre in Hyderabad as AI Race Intensifies
excerpt: The tech giant's fourth Indian cloud region has already signed up Adani Group and HDFC Bank, cementing its lead over rivals Google and Amazon in a market of more than one billion internet users.
body:
• Microsoft launched its India South Central data centre in Hyderabad, its largest facility in the country and fourth cloud region after Pune, Chennai and Mumbai.
  • Adani Group and HDFC Bank are among the first enterprise customers to sign on to the new facility.
  • The company has committed roughly $20.5 billion to expand its India operations, betting on AI demand and a deep pool of tech talent.
  • Azure has posted double-digit revenue growth in India for two consecutive years.

Microsoft on Thursday launched its largest data centre hub in India, opening the India South Central facility in Hyderabad as it races to cement its lead over Alphabet and Amazon in one of the world's fastest-growing cloud and artificial intelligence markets.

The new facility brings the Windows maker's cloud regions in India to four, adding to existing centres in Pune, Chennai and Mumbai. Adani Group and HDFC Bank are among the early enterprise users, Microsoft said, underscoring the depth of demand from both conglomerates and financial institutions for locally hosted cloud infrastructure.

A $20.5 Billion Bet on India

Microsoft has committed about $20.5 billion to expand its India operations, drawn by a market of more than one billion internet users and what the company calls one of the world's deepest pools of technology talent. Azure, its cloud-computing arm, has posted double-digit revenue increases in the country for the last two years.

"Creating value with AI requires trusted infrastructure close to where data lives, teams work and decisions are made. This facility is a critical part of that foundation."

— Puneet Chandok, President, Microsoft India

Beyond its own data centres, Microsoft also operates two facilities in partnership with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio, reinforcing its strategy of blending direct investment with local alliances.

Hyderabad's Growing Tech Footprint

The choice of Hyderabad reflects Telangana's rising profile as a technology hub. The state's software exports have grown steadily, and it already hosts a large Microsoft Development Centre. The company has partnered with the Telangana government on cloud adoption and AI upskilling programmes for government officials.

The new cloud region will offer the full Microsoft portfolio — Azure, AI, productivity tools and CRM — with advanced data security. It also adds disaster-recovery resilience to Microsoft's Indian network, complementing the Azure Availability Zones launched earlier in its Central India region.

Rivals Pour In

Microsoft is not alone in its pursuit of the Indian market. Alphabet's Google, in partnership with Adani Group and Airtel, has announced a $15 billion investment to build a 1-gigawatt AI data centre in Visakhapatnam. Amazon Web Services has also been expanding capacity. Not all of these efforts have proceeded smoothly — environmentalists have accused authorities of fast-tracking a planned Google data centre without adequately weighing risks to water supplies and wildlife, allegations the government has denied.

Why It Matters for Indian Tech Workers Abroad

For the roughly five million Indian-origin professionals working in the global technology sector, the expansion signals a broadening of high-value AI and cloud roles in India. Microsoft already employs 22,000 AI engineers in the country and continues to hire, with the vast majority of its India job openings requiring AI skills. The buildup of local infrastructure also strengthens the case for enterprises — Indian and multinational alike — to process sensitive data within the country rather than routing it through overseas servers.

With data sovereignty regulations tightening worldwide, domestic cloud capacity is increasingly a competitive advantage. Microsoft's aggressive push suggests it sees India not just as a consumer of cloud services but as a critical node in its global AI infrastructure.
